title: Paper Awards, Real Trucks: Pricing the U.S. 2027 Truckload Bid Season
summary: U.S. 2027 truckload RFPs are landing in a tight market. How carriers and brokers pick lanes, set rates, and write fuel and accessorial terms that hold up.
body_markdown:
The email lands at 7:12 a.m. on the Monday before Thanksgiving. Subject line: "2027 Truckload RFP, Round 1. Responses due Dec. 11."


You're the pricing lead at a mid-size U.S. hybrid operation. About 180 tractors on the asset side, a brokerage desk down the hall. You open the attachment.


It's 1,140 lanes, rates effective Feb. 1. There's a fuel tab, an accessorial tab, and a column that wants a weekly truck count on every lane you bid.


Then you notice row 412. You won that lane last year. By June you were rejecting most of its tenders, because the rate stopped making sense once the market turned.


This shipper remembers. So should you.


(The operator is illustrative. The market is not.)


## The market you're bidding into


A national dry van contract rate measure sat around $2.88 a mile, excluding fuel, in mid-November 2026, per industry rate data reported Nov. 13. That's up roughly 25% from a year earlier.


What it means: last year's rate is not your anchor. Repeat it and you're volunteering to haul at a loss, or to reject loads later.


Government data agrees. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price index for long-distance truckload freight ran about 25% above year-ago levels in October 2026 (preliminary). This isn't one data source's quirk. Prices have reset.


Carriers are also saying no more often. The national truckload tender rejection rate ran near 12.9% in mid-November, per the same industry data. That's roughly double the year-ago level.


What it means: about one contracted load in eight gets turned down. Shippers feel that, and it shapes what they'll ask of you.


The October 2026 Logistics Managers' Index, released Nov. 3, put transportation capacity at 38.0. Anything under 50 means contraction. So the trucks just aren't there.


This isn't a buyer's market or a seller's market. It's a capacity market. Every cell in that spreadsheet really asks one thing: will a truck show up?


## The award that didn't stick


Go back to row 412.


Last winter you priced it to win. The market was soft and you needed volume. By spring, spot paid more than your contract, your planners found better freight, and acceptance on that lane slid week by week.


You weren't alone. One large brokerage's Q3 2026 market report said contract rates set early in the 2026 bid season "proved too low." Mini-bid activity spiked, and some shippers rebid their entire book.


The same report put primary tender acceptance in its network at 78% in August 2026. In the prior three years it ran 90% to 94%.


What it means: a lot of 2026 awards were paper, and shippers paid for them.


They paid real money. When a load falls to the second carrier in the routing guide, it costs about 9.3% more, per industry data reported Nov. 16. At the third tender or beyond, the premium is 17.6%.


So shippers now know exactly what a broken award costs. Expect them to score your past acceptance in this bid, not just your rate.


## What's actually in the spreadsheet


Read the RFP tabs like a contract, because that's what they become.


**Capacity commitments.** Shippers want a weekly truck count per lane, and many will score you on it. A low rate with a commitment of one truck a week doesn't cover a five-load lane.


**Their fuel schedule, not yours.** Most bids ask you to price linehaul only and accept the shipper's fuel table. That makes bids comparable. It also means the fuel tab can quietly decide your margin.


**A standard accessorial schedule.** Detention, layover, stop-offs, driver assist, truck ordered not used. Shippers increasingly want these fixed up front, with exceptions disclosed in the bid.


**Tender lead time and appointment rules.** Notice hours, live or drop, receiving windows.


**Index-linked or shorter-term options.** Some shippers offer rates that float with a published market index, or terms shorter than a year. If you see one, ask which index, how often it resets, and whether there's a floor. Others say plainly they'll mini-bid any lane where acceptance drops.


That last point is worth taking seriously. A September 2026 survey of 53 shipper supply chain professionals found only 25% use defined rules to decide which lanes go to annual contract, short-term deals, mini-tenders, indexed pricing or spot. The authors called the results directional, given the small sample.


What it means: three out of four shippers decide lane strategy on judgment. Your past performance on their freight is a big part of that judgment. So is how clearly you say what you can't commit to.


## The drivers you can't promise


Before you promise anyone a truck, look at your own seats. The U.S. Department of Transportation said on Nov. 4, 2026, that 33,000 commercial drivers had been placed out of service for failing English language proficiency requirements since April 2025. That's up from 26,000 reported in August. DOT didn't publish a detailed breakdown of how the total was calculated.


What it means: a driver who fails a roadside check is out of service on the spot. Every lane that driver covers becomes a lane you can't run.


The non-domiciled CDL rule is the slower squeeze. FMCSA's final rule took effect March 16, 2026. It limits non-domiciled CDLs to drivers in H-2A, H-2B or E-2 status, with credentials that last a year at most.


FMCSA itself estimated roughly 194,000 current holders would exit freight over about five years as credentials come up for renewal. The challenge in the D.C. Circuit (Lujan v. FMCSA) was argued Sept. 15, and the docket still showed no merits decision as of Nov. 20.


What it means: a capacity commitment you sign in December may rest on drivers whose licenses expire in March. Pull your roster by license expiration before you write a single truck count in that column.


## Fuel: the tab that can eat the linehaul


You flip to the fuel tab. It's the shipper's table, with a peg price and a cents-per-mile step for every few cents diesel moves.


The U.S. Energy Information Administration put the national average on-highway diesel price at $5.937 a gallon for the week of Nov. 16, 2026. That's down from $6.292 two weeks earlier, but still $2.069 higher than a year ago.


What it means: diesel has moved more in a year than many fuel tables were designed to handle.


EIA's November Short-Term Energy Outlook, released Nov. 10, forecast retail diesel averaging $5.03 a gallon in 2027. That forecast is 12% higher than the agency's October number.


What it means: even government forecasters keep revising fuel up. Don't bank on relief.


Do the simple math before you accept the table. At 6.5 miles per gallon (use your own fleet's number), every $1 move in diesel is about 15 cents a mile in fuel cost. Then check what the shipper's table actually pays at $5, $6 and $7 diesel.


If the table lags your real cost per mile, your linehaul has to cover the gap. Price it in, or note an exception. Don't just accept it and hope.


Check the index and cadence too. Weekly national and monthly regional tables behave differently. West Coast diesel ran $6.948 that same week, a big gap if your lanes live out west.


## Deciding which lanes to bid


Not every lane deserves a number. Sort the 1,140 into three piles.


**Lanes your network wants.** They build density, reload near your drivers' homes, or fix an imbalance. Bid these with conviction and a real commitment.


**Lanes you could run at the right price.** They don't hurt the network, but they don't help it either. Bid them at a rate that pays for the truck as a standalone move. If you lose them, fine.


**Lanes that only work on paper.** One-way into a dead market, erratic volume, long dwell. Don't low-bid these to look helpful. Decline them, or hand them to the brokerage desk with a broker's margin and honest capacity language.


For a hybrid shop, that third pile matters most. If the asset side bids a lane it can't really cover, the brokerage desk ends up covering it at spot. That's how one division quietly subsidizes the other.


Then set the rate. Start from today's true cost per mile. Add expected dwell per facility and the empty miles the lane really creates. Only then decide what to give back for network value.


Remember the market's signal. Contract renewals were averaging 12% to 13% above prior rates in November, per industry data, against a five-year average near 3.5%.


What it means: a renewal well under that needs a reason, like density or a lane you badly want. "We want to keep the account" isn't a reason. It's how row 412 happened.


## The fine print that pays the bills


You skip back to the accessorial tab, because this is where winning bids lose money.


Write detention free time, hourly rates, layover, TONU and stop-offs into the bid. If the shipper's schedule is too thin, disclose the exception now, not after the first short-paid invoice.


Tie every accessorial to proof: timestamps, appointment confirmations, approval rules. A charge you quoted and can document is a charge you can collect.


Watch the volume language too. A commitment should be a range or a defined weekly quantity, with rules for surges. Promising 100% of a lane's freight when the shipper's own forecast swings wildly is how acceptance drops in May.


## Before you hit submit


Run this list on every bid this season:


-


**Roster check.** Match committed trucks to drivers whose licenses, medical cards and English proficiency are solid through the contract term.


-


**True-cost floor.** No lane below your current all-in cost per mile, including empty miles and expected dwell.


-


**Fuel stress test.** Model the shipper's table at three diesel prices and record any shortfall in your linehaul or exceptions.


-


**Accessorial exceptions.** Disclose every term you can't live with, in writing, inside the bid.


-


**Honest commitments.** Commit a truck count you'd still honor if spot jumps 30%.


-


**Asset vs. brokerage split.** Decide which division owns each lane before the award, not after.


-


**Mini-bid readiness.** Know your walk-away rate per lane so you can answer a 48-hour mini-bid without a meeting.


## The award letter, and what comes after


The award arrives in late January. You won fewer lanes than last year. That's fine. You won lanes you can run.


Now make it hold. For 30, 60 and 90 days, track acceptance by lane, awarded versus accepted volume, and invoice variance against the bid. If a lane slips, you want to see it in week three, not June.


Row 412 isn't in the award. You declined to bid it below cost, and you told the shipper why. They called back in March asking about a mini-bid at a rate that actually works.


## Make your system match the bid


No two bids look alike, and no two networks do either.


One RFP is 40 tight-appointment lanes. Another is 1,100 one-way lanes with a fuel table from another era. A third wants index pricing on half its book.


The shops that come out of bid season with margin aren't the ones with the cheapest rates. They're the ones whose systems know how their freight actually behaves.


Rate tables that carry each customer's own fuel and accessorial terms. Statuses that flag a rejected tender on a contract lane. Permissions that stop a broker quoting below the asset side's floor. Capacity logic tied to real drivers and license dates. Billing rules that know which detention terms belong to which award.


That setup work is unglamorous. It's also what turns a paper award into freight you actually haul, at a rate you actually keep.


## FAQ


### When does the 2027 truckload contract bid season run?


Most U.S. shippers run annual truckload bids from November through the first quarter, so new rates start with the calendar or fiscal year. Many shippers also run mini-bids during the year on lanes that stop performing.


### How much are truckload contract rates rising for 2027?


Contract renewals were averaging 12% to 13% above prior rates in November 2026, per industry data, so double-digit increases are a realistic starting point. A national dry van contract measure sat near $2.88 a mile excluding fuel, about 25% above a year earlier.


### Why do carriers reject tenders on lanes they were awarded?


Carriers reject awarded tenders when the contract rate falls below what the truck can earn elsewhere or the lane no longer fits their network. In 2026, many awards priced in a soft market stopped holding once capacity tightened.


### Should a carrier accept the shipper's fuel surcharge table?


Accept a shipper's fuel table only after testing what it pays at several diesel prices against your real cost per mile. EIA put diesel at $5.937 a gallon for the week of Nov. 16, 2026, so a table built for cheaper fuel can quietly eat your linehaul.


### How do driver compliance rules affect bid commitments?


Driver compliance rules reduce the trucks you can safely promise, because an out-of-service driver or an expiring non-domiciled CDL can empty a seat mid-contract. Check every committed lane against your roster's license and qualification dates before you submit truck counts.
